items.title: Christian Leaders Call America to 52 Days of Prayer and Repentance
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's not political."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Barbara Ann Jeter is the executive director of the Nehemiah Alliance, a movement pushing Americans toward “prayer, fasting, repentance, and national spiritual renewal.”

Jeter told CBN News the effort was birthed from an “inquiry of God last August.”

“[I asked], ‘What do you want, Lord, for America’s 250th?'” she said, noting she believes the Lord provided a path forward.

Jeter found herself sending a plan to national leaders she trusted, building the Nehemiah Alliance platform on the pattern seen in the Book of Nehemiah.

“Like Nehemiah sought the blessing of his pagan foreign king and governors along the way when he was rebuilding the walls, we have sought the blessing and gotten it from those in authority,” she said. “It’s not political, but there is something about getting the blessing of those that God’s placed in authority.”

Ultimately, Jeter was able to rally not just political leaders of the day like House Speaker Mike Johnson, but she has mobilized well-known Christian figures like Alveda King, Michael W. Smith, and Eric Metaxas, among many others, to not only support the effort but also to show up Oct. 31 for a massive event in Washington, D.C.

“We want to mobilize the people for 52 days of prayer, fasting, and repentance,” she said. “It’s historic. It’s never been done. We started Sunday on 9/10. I heard 9/11. God starts His calendar, I believe, the night before, and we’re going to All Saints Sunday. We’ll be on the National Mall. We believe it is a Nehemiah call to the wall — to the Mall — to rebuild our spiritual walls.”

Jeter said she chose Oct. 31, which is both Reformation Day and Halloween, to hold the culminating event.

“On the darkest night, we’re believing to shine the brightest light, the light of the world all over the world,” she said. “That’s Jesus.”

Even though the prayer and fasting commitment started a month ago, Jeter said it’s not too late for people to jump in now, especially since Oct. 31 is still weeks away.

“Fast as the Holy Spirit leads you,” Jeter said. “We definitely want people fasting the day of Halloween.”

In addition to prayer and fasting, she said she’s also “calling people to commit to be a modern-day gatekeeper.”

“Remember in the Bible, in Nehemiah, they built that wall in front of their own house? You’re gonna build it stronger if you’re building it in front of where you are,” she said. “Pray for your own family, your neighborhood, your local schools, your pastors. Pray for leaders and those in authority … pray for these upcoming elections.”

Jeter said she wants people to walk away from this effort with a renewed heart aimed at turning individuals, families, and culture back to Jesus. She also wants people to attend the event on the National Mall on Oct. 31.

“Come,” she said. “Answer your call to the Mall to rebuild our spiritual walls.”

items.title: Biblical Archaeology Disproves ‘Very Odd’ Claim About Modern Israel, Dinesh D’Souza Says
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "Political significance."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

As Americans’ favorability toward the modern state of Israel continues to wax and wane, as antisemitism swells, and as allegations of genocide ring out, author and commentator Dinesh D’Souza is making the case that history is on the side of the Jewish state.

Biblical archaeology, D’Souza recently told CBN News, “irrefutably shows the presence of the Jews in their ancient homeland.”

D’Souza’s comments, as well as the release of his new book, “The Stones Cry Out: Biblical Archaeology, Prophecy, and the Last Days,” come at a time when U.S. citizens are deeply divided — even in conservative and Christian circles — over Israel.

Data from the Pew Research Center shows Americans’ favorability toward both the Israeli government and its people is on the decline, with 62% holding unfavorable views toward the Jewish state’s government. Additionally, antisemitism has been on the rise in the U.S. since the Hamas-led attack against Israel in October 2023.

The Anti-Defamation League tracked a huge spike in antisemitic attacks in 2024 and, while those numbers fell somewhat in 2025, they have remained historically high. For context, the ADL recorded 6,274 incidents last year, a 33% drop from 2024 but still the third-highest total since the organization began tracking such incidents in 1979.

It’s not only an issue in America, either. Just this week, news broke of a hotel in Dublin reportedly canceling a reservation for 70 rooms for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after its administrators learned the purpose of their visit. Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told The Times of Israel that Herbert Park Hotel initially green-lit the booking for delegates representing the European Union’s 27 member states but later reneged after a phone call with the hotel’s general manager.

Cohen told the outlet he noticed a “manner change” in the manager after telling her the purpose of the meeting in Dublin. He recalled a “tension that had not been there before” when, upon learning the purpose of the event, the general manager asked Cohen if the Israel Defense Forces would be involved in the gathering.

“We were talking about a conference in Dublin on antisemitism, attended by Jewish community representatives, diplomats, civil servants and government officials,” he told The Times. “Nothing I had said had anything whatsoever to do with the Israeli army, yet, somehow, that was where the conversation had gone.”

The manager then purportedly told Cohen she’d have to check with the owners to determine whether the reservation could remain. Apparently, it could not: the rooms were canceled.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, told Fox News the incident “is a disgraceful example of the very antisemitism the conference was organized to combat.”

Much of the hostility toward Israel centers on the claim the Jewish state is committing genocide against Palestinians, a leftist talking point becoming less defensible as new data from the Palestinian Ministry of Health shows the population in Gaza actually grew significantly in 2025. Nevertheless, as CBN News reported, Israel remains on high alert against attacks ahead of its Oct. 27 elections.

D’Souza, for his part, made the case this week that it’s “very odd” to accuse Israelis of seeking to take land that does not belong to them when there is a breadth of archaeological history proving Jewish presence in the land dating back centuries.

“It really irrefutably shows the presence of the Jews in their ancient homeland, going back 3,000, even more than 3,000 years,” he said. “And so the familiar accusation that the Jews are colonizers immediately becomes very odd, right? Because it’s like accusing the Indians of colonizing India or the Irish of colonizing Ireland. How do you colonize your own ancestral homeland?”

To make his case, D’Souza pointed to a 2,000-year-old, 25-ton Jewish ritual bath, known as a mikveh, discovered this summer by the Israel Antiquities Authority. The relic, which was excavated nearly totally intact, provides evidence of a previously unknown Jewish settlement between the Judean Lowlands and the northern Negev, according to the IAA.

“[T]hese ritual baths were used by Jews to kind of cleanse themselves before they went to the temple,” D’Souza explained. “So there is a political significance, I think, to these archaeological exhibits coming out of the ground.”

items.title: Jamie MacDonald Had No Plan for Any of This
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Last year, Jamie MacDonald was in the middle of singing “A Million Chances” at a small radio event when Tori Kelly appeared in the doorway. It was the first time she had really gotten to share her songs live, and her team hadn’t warned her Kelly would be there. They knew she would panic. “I’m…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Last year, Jamie MacDonald was in the middle of singing “A Million Chances” at a small radio event when Tori Kelly appeared in the doorway. It was the first time she had really gotten to share her songs live, and her team hadn’t warned her Kelly would be there. They knew she would panic.

“I’m like, I have to sing in front of Tori Kelly,” MacDonald laughed. Kelly heard her sing the song and tell her testimony, and she told MacDonald it stayed in her head ever since.

A year later, when MacDonald decided to re-release “A Million Chances,” Kelly said she would love to sing on it. Kelly lives in California but was in Nashville, so the two got to record in the same room for a day, which MacDonald said doesn’t always happen with collabs. “Most of us were just sitting there pinching ourselves as we watched her do her thing,” she said. “She just blew us all away.”

The new “A Million Chances” is one of 30 tracks on Jamie MacDonald (The Deluxe Album), which is out now. MacDonald calls Kelly and Lauren Daigle, who also appears on the project, “two heroes of mine,” and said landing them was “something I didn’t even dream for myself.”

It’s a lot for someone who, by her own count, had never played a show a year and a half ago. Her self-titled debut album came out in January, and “Desperate,” “Left It in the River” and “Ain’t No Way” each went to No. 1 at Christian radio. This fall she is playing arenas on Phil Wickham’s tour, and she recently won New Artist of the Year at the Dove Awards.

Ten years hidden

About two years ago, MacDonald was posting on social media roughly once a year. “I wasn’t trying for the artist thing at all,” she said. A label would normally never sign someone with no singing on her Instagram, she pointed out, because nothing about it looked like she wanted to make music.

She calls the decade before that a hidden season. “It was a time of healing and being hidden for me for the past ten years or even longer, where God was still working out the story and bringing me peace with my story before it was time to tell it.” In her Dove Awards acceptance speech, she talked about waiting tables and recovering from addiction, and about how CeCe Winans’ music helped change her life.

She had tried the Christian label route years earlier and never found where she fit. “I’m doing the same exact style now, but it fits,” she said. “I think it’s God’s timing.” And she doesn’t think she would have felt ready on her own. “If I was waiting till I felt ready, it might have been never.”

The songs have a goal, she said. “God snatched me out of the fire and out of a really dark past. That’s why I have such a passion for souls with my music.”

“Desperate,” her first radio single, was the first time she saw it work. She called it a deeper cry of grief, a song she needed, and the response told her plenty of other people did too. “Suddenly I wasn’t walking alone anymore through my grief,” she said. “Music can be medicine.”

“Left It in the River” came out of her baptism. She remembers coming up from the water “shame free and washed clean and delivered,” and she said the song matched that feeling. A lot of people have told her it inspired them to get baptized.

Singing all of it night after night took some practice. Some songs on the album are about things she had never talked about or grieved, and last year there were nights she couldn’t get through them. It’s getting easier now that she can look out and see people singing along as if the songs are theirs. “It’s hard to cry and sing at the same time,” she joked.

There are five — count ’em, five — versions of “Left It in the River” on the deluxe, including a soul version. MacDonald said the extra material is to show where she came from and reflect more of her personal style than just the radio version.

“We gotta give the people the radio version,” she said, “but then I’m like, let’s give a little bit more flavor of where I came from.” Which is why you’ll hear influences from her love of Mariah Carey, Lauryn Hill, Whitney Houston and ’70s soul. The deluxe also adds two new songs, a Daigle version of “Desperate” and a run of acoustic, live and studio-session cuts.

items.title: ‘Spare Us Yet’: Short Stories of Catholicism, COVID, and Cancellation
items.author: Jonathan Mittiga
items.summary:
Jonathan Mittiga

Faith sits quietly within each story, shaping how the characters confront their moral predicaments without necessarily resolving them.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Jonathan Mittiga

“Every society is a theocracy. Figure out what people have made into God, and their society snaps into focus.”

This line comes from Mr. Humberstone, a character in Lucas Smith’s 2025 short-story collection, Spare Us Yet and Other Stories (Wiseblood Books). Mr. Humberstone, a young academic and journalist, stands accused by an online mob of raping his ex-“girlfriend” (with girlfriend serving perhaps as too concrete a term; “They liked to keep it vague,” the narrator explains). 

In light of the controversy, Mr. Humberstone’s editor asks him to take leave from work, and he returns to his mother’s house, presumably to stew over the injustice he’s been dealt. In that way, the story offers a sort of behind-the-scenes of modern-day “cancel culture.” However, instead of actually fixating on the concept of “guilty until proven innocent,” Mr. Humberstone prays—for his ex-girlfriend, for her mother, and for the people accusing him. 

“He was pursuing a subjective state of well-being through the feeling of faith,” the narrator explains. “The important thing was to know that God was real no matter what he thought.” Yet he still reaches a human limit: “Knowing this did not make him feel better.”

This story, “Mr. Humberstone’s Trial,” finds the character at the end of a reluctant Christian conversion. “He passed what he thought was his excusable Marxist phase and his liberal humanist phase,” the narrator explains, only to find himself drawn, as if by an “irresistible force” to “eternal Christendom.” “Oh shit,” he thinks to himself. “I’m a Christian. Oh shit, oh shit, shit, shit, shit.” He writes a letter to his girlfriend explaining his conversion: “In a way, I can. In a way, I can’t.” Ultimately, words fail, and his endless reasoning is reduced to the virtue of faith.

Mr. Humberstone has changed his stance on premarital sex, for example, as a result of his conversion, and he expresses his wish to abstain—a desire that sits in stark contrast with the accusation against him. The “trial” mentioned in the title therefore refers not so much to a literal trial in court as to a trial of penitential suffering—the trial of a new Christian whose faith is being tested.

This is the strange moral territory Smith explores in Spare Us Yet. His characters are confused, compromised, and often wrong. They live in a world shaped by bureaucracies, online mobs, lockdowns, broken families, and political resentment. But, interestingly, Smith is not especially concerned with settling ideological arguments or telling us which side is right. He is more interested in how imperfect people reach for God.

On that score, the title Spare Us Yet recalls the Parce Domine of the Latin liturgy, “Spare, O Lord, spare thy people.” It is a plea to God to spare his people according to his mercy rather than punish them according to their offenses, and to deliver them in times of spiritual trial. These references do not exist within Smith’s stories simply to announce that the author is Catholic; Catholicism, for Smith, is not wallpaper. Instead, they provide windows into the interior lives of the characters, giving them a vocabulary for experiences that modern political language cannot adequately describe.

Likewise, the characters are not saints, and Catholicism is not a shallow evangelization device. Instead, faith sits quietly within each story, shaping how the characters confront their moral predicaments without necessarily resolving them. Each character reaches for it imperfectly in the search for truth.

In making sense of this dynamic, it’s helpful to think of the collection’s preface, “Prelude: Unit 1002,” as a frame for the stories that follow. In “Prelude: Unit 1002,” a nameless angel is called down with great fanfare to protect Christ’s altar. But this occurs in 1858, and the novel takes place during COVID. In the years that follow, the church is slowly abandoned—yet bureaucratic rules keep the angel from being released despite the abandonment, and he finds himself in the same storage unit into which the altar is placed. Eventually, he is released when the storage unit itself is abandoned and then sold to the highest bidder. Upon the sale, the altar is fed into a woodchipper, finally freeing the beleaguered angel from his earthly duties. Thus, the altar meets a darkly comic end. “Lord, have mercy on them!” the angel says as he ascends back to heaven. 

It is a strange and funny story but also a sad one—and it captures a paradox of the period Smith documents. Despite trending urban parishes and occasional sexy optics, the Church Militant—the living body of believers on earth fighting against sin, temptation, and the devil—has long been shrinking in cultural influence. Yet even as churches closed during COVID, Catholicism was acquiring a certain cultural cachet, particularly among young writers, artists, and intellectuals. Its institutional presence was appearing diminished at precisely the moment its aesthetics, traditions, and moral vocabulary were becoming newly fashionable. 

During the COVID lockdowns, this institutional decline became literal: Churches closed, public worship was restricted, and religious life was treated by governments as one more activity eligible for suspension—even as liquor stores remained open for business. COVID was topical when Smith’s stories were written, but, unfortunately, it remains relevant to understanding the current state of the church in larger culture today as well. 

Amid the lockdowns, the question of vaccination mandates in particular divided society: Should individuals be free to decline vaccination, or should governments be able to require it? This is another lens through which Smith investigates moral dilemmas. 

In “Lions Over the Bridge,” Smith follows a homeless man whose situation stems from his COVID-vaccine refusal. It would be easy to turn this character into a political martyr: an innocent man destroyed by an unjust system. But Smith refuses to make things that simple. The man is troubled in his own right. “HOMELESS DUE TO JAB,” he writes on a cardboard box as he begs on the street, even as he refuses his brother’s offer of a room. His suffering may be real, as may the forces acting against him, but this does not mean every decision he makes is reasonable. Yet he still reaches for truth, even using a quote he attributes to St. Isaac the Syrian: “Be like the bees and go where the good stuff is.” 

In his homeless, jobless wanderings, he casts judgement. He presses his diocese’s archbishop for forcing priests “to take the jab.” His mind is addled with diversions, and he pontificates, “You can’t pray ironically, and you can’t pray as if you are right. Prayer must always leave open the possibility you are wrong.” 

Smith’s characters are three-dimensional, and each of them—whether chasing after atheist graffiti artists, planning illicit Shrove Tuesday gatherings, or altar-serving at empty funeral Masses at the height of “stop the spread”—retains the possibility of an act of grace. Flannery O’Connor once described her own subject in fiction as “the action of grace in territory largely held by the devil.” Smith works in similar territory. His characters are never beyond the reach of mercy. And whereas O’Connor often ushers in grace through grotesque comedy, violence, or a sudden reversal, “Lions Over the Bridge” arrives at its own strange reversal.

The COVID years have been “memory-holed,” and when recalled, they are remembered differently by opposing political factions with conveniently alternative memories. Smith remembers something strange that he illustrates through his fiction: human beings trying to remain human while isolation, bureaucracy, and ideology reshape their society and their lives. 

Vitriol and pedantic moralization do not spew from these stories. There is no long anti-vaccine tract disguised as dialogue, nor are the characters merely puppets Smith uses to convert readers to Catholicism. Instead, Catholicism provides a language for sin, suffering, forgiveness, and grace without making any of those virtues easy. A challenging collection, Spare Us Yet rewards close rereading, with each story rich enough to warrant a review of its own. 

Still, complications linger. Even though much of its subject matter will resonate with those who lived through the COVID years, readers may not always know immediately what Smith wants them to make of a story. A few stories require a rereading before they can be fully absorbed. Individual lines can carry an unusual amount of weight, and, for better or worse, Smith often refuses to provide the moral conclusion that a less confident writer might underline at the end.

This density works better in some stories than in others. There were moments that demanded slightly more clarity. But the difficulty also seems inseparable from what Smith is doing. These are stories about people who cannot fully decipher the moral situations they themselves inhabit. Why should the reader be allowed to stand comfortably above them?

Spare Us Yet is not a demand that God punish our enemies. It is not even a confident
declaration that “we were right.” It is a prayer uttered by people who know the world is
disordered, who suspect that they are disordered too, and who can only beg for mercy over judgment. As we emerge from the COVID era and its consequences, Smith offers an important documentation of what occurred, the aftermath we’re still experiencing, the way Catholicism interplays with American life throughout the most unusual seasons, and the way art can still make us human after all.

items.title: Monday, October 19, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today in our Gospel, Jesus tells of a rich man who has been so successful that he doesn’t have enough space to store his harvest.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 2:1-10

You were dead through the trespasses and sins in which you once lived, following the course of this world, following the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work among those who are disobedient. All of us once lived among them in the passions of our flesh, following the desires of flesh and senses, and we were by nature children of wrath, like everyone else. But God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us even when we were dead through our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved— and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, so that in the ages to come he might show the immeasurable riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God— not the result of works, so that no one may boast. For we are what he has made us, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand to be our way of life.

Psalm
Psalm 100:1b-2, 3, 4ab, 4c-5

Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth.
     Worship the Lord with gladness;
    come into his presence with singing.
Know that the Lord is God.
    It is he that made us, and we are his;
    we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
Enter his gates with thanksgiving,
    and his courts with praise.
    Give thanks to him, bless his name.
For the Lord is good;
    his steadfast love endures forever,
    and his faithfulness to all generations.

Gospel Reading
Luke 12:13-21

Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the family inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Friend, who set me to be a judge or arbitrator over you?” And he said to them, “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.” Then he told them a parable: “The land of a rich man produced abundantly. And he thought to himself, ‘What should I do, for I have no place to store my crops?’ Then he said, ‘I will do this: I will pull down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you. And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So it is with those who store up treasures for themselves but are not rich toward God.”

Reflection

Friends, today in our Gospel, Jesus tells of a rich man who has been so successful that he doesn’t have enough space to store his harvest. So he tears down his barns and builds bigger ones. But that very night, he dies—and all of it comes to naught. “Thus will it be for the one who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich in what matters to God.”

No matter how good, how beautiful a state of affairs is here below, it is destined to pass into nonbeing. That sunset that I enjoyed last night—that radiantly beautiful display—is now forever gone. It lasted only a while. That beautiful person—attractive, young, full of life, creative, joyful—will eventually age, get sick, break down, and die.

An image that always comes to mind when I think of these things is the gorgeous firework that bursts open like a giant flower and then, in the twinkling of an eye, is gone forever. Everything is haunted by nonbeing. Everything, finally, is a bubble.

But this is not meant to depress us; it is meant to redirect our attention precisely to the things that are “above,” to the eternity of God.
